newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Bhutto urges conference on Kashmir, S. Asia arms.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto urges conference on Kashmir, S. Asia arms.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto proposed on Thursday convening an ambitious international conference to resolve the long-festering Kashmir dispute with India and halt the danger of a nuclear arms race in South Asia.

In a speech to the General Assembly focusing heavily on the issue of Kashmir, she also warned that, just as Pakistan was prepared to sign any nuclear treaties if India signed simultaneously, "any step of nuclear escalation by our neighbour will find a response from us to preserve our national security."
Both India and Pakistan are believed to have nuclear weapons or the ability to assemble them quickly. India exploded a nuclear device in 1974 which it said was for peaceful purposes.

Bhutto said: "I would like to take this opportunity to propose to this august Assembly that it endorse the convening of a multilateral dialogue for peace and security in South Asia, including the participation of not only Pakistan and India, but of the five permanent members of the Security Council and other major powers like Germany and Japan." The permanent council members are the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France.
Bhutto said the proposed conference could cover three critical areas:
"One - the resolution of the Kashmir dispute and other multilateral problems between India and Pakistan;
"Two - the promotion of conventional arms control and confidence building measures;
"Three - measures to promote nuclear restraint and arrest the danger of a nuclear arms race in South Asia."

Such multilateral talks offer a "framework for genuine negotiations which can lead to resolution of disputes, arrest the nuclear threat and promote prosperity in South Asia. And I hope that this proposal will evoke support in this Assembly and from India," she said.

Bhutto said a Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty endorsed by the General Assembly last month and opened for signature last week was "exactly the kind of global measure for non-proliferation and disarmament" that India had championed for 40 years.

But India "chose to veto the treaty" recently in the Geneva Conference on Disarmament and opposed it when it was brought instead before the U.N. Assembly. The treaty will not enter into force until all 44 countries with nuclear reactors -- including India -- have signed and ratified it.
Indian external Affairs Minister Inder Kumar Gujral is due to address the Assembly on Friday.

Bhutto proposed the international conference the day after telling a closed-door meeting of foreign ministers of the 53-member Organisation of the Islamic Conference that the world "cannot remain indifferent to the rise of a fundamentalist Hindu India bent on producing and deploying nuclear-capable ballistic missiles, with the aim to target every major city from Yemen to the Straits of Malacca."

On the issue of Kashmir, India's only Moslem-majority state, she told the 185-member General Assembly its people were still awaiting fulfilment of a 50-year-old U.N. decision that their future should be decided through a plebiscite.
"So I stand before the assembled United Nations and urge, 'to thine own self be true,'" she said, adding that there was no statute of limitations on U.N. resolutions.

Referring to an uprising against Indian rule in Kashmir that erupted nearly seven years ago, she said Indian soldiers resorted to murder, torture, rape, persecution, arson, incarceration and assassination attempts.

India sought last month to "divert world opinion by organising a sham election," she said, adding: "Those very people who claim to be front runners in the elections cannot even enter the (Kashmir) valley without armed escorts, much less muster popular support."
